query: What additive manufacturing strategy and post-processing route can enable the fabrication of a refractory high-entropy alloy family (Group IV-V transition metals) capable of retaining high-temperature structural integrity, and what specific microstructural state is hypothesized to optimize mechanical performance while mitigating the inherent brittleness associated with interstitial impurities?

generation.hypothesis: Fabrication of a Group IV-V refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20 or NbMoTaW) via Laser Powder Bed Fusion (PBF-LB/M) or Selective Laser Melting (SLM), followed by a high-temperature annealing post-processing route, can enable the retention of high-temperature structural integrity. The hypothesized optimal microstructural state is a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with a refined, homogeneous dendritic/cellular microstructure and minimized interstitial impurity (O, N, C) content. This state is expected to optimize mechanical performance by mitigating the inherent brittleness associated with interstitial impurities, which otherwise form ordered complexes that pin dislocations and reduce ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Powder mixture of Group IV-V transition metals (W, Mo, Ta, Nb, V) or (Nb, Mo, Ta, W) with inherent interstitial impurities (O, N, C) from raw materials and processing atmosphere.
generation.intervention: Additive manufacturing via Laser Powder Bed Fusion (PBF-LB/M) or Selective Laser Melting (SLM) using optimized linear energy density (e.g., ≥2.83 J/mm) to achieve in-situ alloy formation and single-phase BCC solid solution, followed by high-temperature annealing to homogenize microstructure and reduce interstitial impurity effects.
generation.conditions: High-temperature service environment (e.g., aerospace, chemical industry) requiring structural integrity; additive manufacturing parameters optimized for full fusion and density >99.8%; post-processing annealing to mitigate interstitial-induced brittleness.
generation.structural_mediator: Single-phase BCC solid solution with refined dendritic/cellular microstructure and reduced interstitial impurity concentration (minimized ordered interstitial complexes).
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy of the multi-principal element alloy stabilizes the single-phase BCC structure. Additive manufacturing enables rapid solidification, forming a fine microstructure. Post-processing annealing homogenizes the structure and reduces the detrimental effects of interstitial impurities (O, N, C) by minimizing their clustering into ordered complexes that impede dislocation motion and cause brittleness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Enhanced high-temperature mechanical performance (strength, ductility, creep resistance) and structural integrity, with mitigated brittleness compared to conventionally processed or un-annealed additive manufactured counterparts.
generation.baseline: Conventionally processed refractory HEAs or additive manufactured refractory HEAs without optimized post-processing, which suffer from processing challenges, coarse microstructures, and interstitial-induced brittleness.
generation.boundary: Applicable to refractory HEAs composed of Group IV-V transition metals (W, Mo, Ta, Nb, V, Hf, Zr) where single-phase BCC formation is thermodynamically favorable; limited by the ability to control interstitial impurity levels during powder production and additive manufacturing.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal annealing temperature and duration to fully mitigate interstitial effects without causing grain coarsening or phase decomposition is uncertain. The long-term stability of the single-phase BCC structure under extreme high-temperature service conditions requires further validation.
generation.falsification_experiment: Fabricate W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20 via PBF-LB/M with and without post-processing annealing. Measure interstitial impurity content (O, N, C) and mechanical properties (tensile strength, ductility, creep resistance) at elevated temperatures. If annealing does not significantly improve ductility or if interstitial impurities remain high and cause brittleness, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.

This is a feature associated with the variety of interstitial relaxation processes involved in these massive solid solutions ( [28] ). Because of the complexity in alloy composition and the resulting multitude in local chemical environments in which the interstitial atoms switch their positions, it is difficult to conduct a complete peak deconvolution analysis based on all possible individual relaxation processes. However, two main configurations of the interstitial atoms can indeed be distinguished in the current material, namely, position switches of interstitials in ordered interstitial complexes and relaxation of randomly distributed interstitial atoms ( [22] ). High entropy or multi principal element alloys are a promising and relatively young concept for designing alloys. The idea of creating alloys without a single main alloying element opens up a wide space for possible new alloy compositions. High entropy alloys based on refractory metals such as W, Mo, Ta or Nb are of interest for future high temperature applications e.g., in the aerospace or chemical industry. However, producing refractory metal high entropy alloys by conventional metallurgical methods remains challenging. For this reason, the feasibility of laser-based additive manufacturing of the refractory metal high entropy alloy W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 by laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) is investigated in the present work. In-situ alloy formation from mixtures of easily available elemental powders is employed to avoid an expensive atomization of pre-alloyed powder. It is shown that PBF-LB/M of W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 is in general possible and that a complete fusion of the powder mixture without a significant number of undissolved particles is achievable by in-situ alloy formation during PBF-LB/M when selecting favorable process parameter combinations. High entropy alloys and related compositions are a relatively young concept for designing alloys. The formation of such multi component alloys was reported independently by Cantor et al. [ [1] ] and the research group around J.-W. Yeh in 2004 [ [2] , [3] , [4] ]. In contrast to most conventional alloys, high entropy alloys do not possess a single main alloying element but comprise a composition of multiple principal elements. The exact definition of high entropy alloys varies from source to source. The most common definition includes alloys consisting of at least five elements with a concentration between 5% and 35% each [ [5] ]. Other definitions demand a configurational entropy of at least 1.5 R [ [6] ]. However, both definitions are overlapping in large parts. Additionally, further criterions like the formation of a single phase solid solution were suggested [ [7] ]. These definitions are discussed extensively in recent review papers [ [7] ] and books [ [6] , [8] ]. The focus of the present work lies on the alloy W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 , which is considered a high entropy alloy in agreement with all these criterions.
